summary: A consultant-level review of ICU sedation and delirium trials. For antipsychotics, MIND-USA (NEJM 2018) and AID-ICU (NEJM 2022) found that haloperidol does not shorten delirium or increase days alive out of hospital. AID-ICU's secondary outcome of mortality was lower with haloperidol at 90 days (36.3 vs 43.3 percent) and at one year, which is a signal, not proof. Prophylactic haloperidol (REDUCE) did not help. For dexmedetomidine, SPICE III showed no overall mortality difference, but a post hoc Bayesian analysis suggested benefit over 65 and harm at 65 or under, which led to a 2022 safety letter agreed with the MHRA. MENDS2 found no difference from propofol in sepsis, and the UK A2B trial (JAMA 2025) found no faster extubation with dexmedetomidine or clonidine compared with propofol, with more agitation and bradycardia. NONSEDA found no advantage for no sedation over light sedation. Pro-MEDIC and the meta-analysis restricted to low risk-of-bias trials found no delirium benefit from melatonin. ABCDEF evidence is mostly observational. R2D2-ICU (JAMA 2026) found that avoiding routine wrist restraints did not increase self-extubation. BRAIN-ICU links longer delirium to lasting cognitive impairment. The 2025 PADIS focused update suggests dexmedetomidine over propofol and suggests melatonin, but it was published before A2B. UK guidance (NICE CG103 and GPICS V3, 2026) does not name a sedative, and UK practice remains propofol first. SESAR (JAMA 2025) found worse survival with sevoflurane than with propofol in ARDS.
takeaways: Aim for light sedation with a daily look at a sedation hold; NONSEDA doesn't justify deeper sedation or no sedation.
Propofol remains a reasonable first-line sedative: A2B found no faster extubation with dexmedetomidine or clonidine, and more agitation and bradycardia.
If using dexmedetomidine, consider age: the SPICE III signal and the 2022 safety letter point to caution in patients 65 or younger.
Haloperidol doesn't shorten delirium and shouldn't be used as prophylaxis; short courses for distress are reasonable, and AID-ICU is reassuring on safety.
Melatonin is cheap and probably harmless, but the best trials show no delirium benefit; put effort into the bundle (mobilisation, sleep, family, fewer restraints).
